abstract: Whole-genome duplication (WGD) through polyploidization has played a major role in genome evolution across eukaryotes. While many well-studied WGDs involve allopolyploidization, autopolyploidization provides a distinct context because duplicated chromosomes initially originate from within the same species and retain high sequence similarity. A major consequence of WGD is the rewiring of gene regulatory networks, partly driven by selection on gene expression dosage. In multicellular organisms, evidence for dosage balance selection has relied largely on comparative patterns of duplicate gene retention and expression, with few studies directly examining regulatory architecture after WGD. Here, we analyzed a large-scale eQTL dataset from Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar), which experienced a salmonid-specific autopolyploid WGD approximately 80 to 100 million years ago. We found that trans-regulatory connections were preferentially retained between WGD-derived syntenic regions and that syntenic trans-eQTL pairs showed elevated three-dimensional genomic contact, suggesting partial preservation of spatial proximity between duplicated chromosomal regions. Overall, 230 duplicated gene pairs (5%) shared eQTLs, suggesting conserved regulatory control. Moreover, 16 gene pairs showed genotype-dependent compensatory expression effects mediated by a common regulator, consistent with predictions of the dosage balance hypothesis. These gene pairs were significantly enriched in late-rediploidizing regions. Our results indicate that a small subset of duplicated genes have retained dosage-balanced regulatory architecture long after WGD.
